     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "0:35", "note": "Title card over the cafeteria wall clock."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "0:36", "note": "Title card over a hallway transformation shimmer."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Say the title word for word by 0:40 at the latest, and earlier (around 0:15) if the cold open is a single gag. Overlay the title card on a wide establishing shot of the episode's main set. Vary the pivot wording each episode, but always state that the mechanism comes next."},
   {"id": "T2", "name": "Scope widening second question",
    "description": "An optional second question that widens what is possible (from 'anyone' to 'anything'). It promises variety in the perk montage.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "0:38", "note": "Widens from people to objects."}],
    "frequency": "1/3",
    "reuse": "Use it when the power has a hidden second dimension (objects as well as people, past as well as future). Keep it to one sentence."}
  ],

  "mechanism": [
   {"id": "M1", "name": "What changes / what stays the same",
    "description": "The mechanism is stated in 2-4 plain sentences that name exactly which part of you changes, then explicitly what stays normal. The thing that stays normal is the planted limit and becomes the main problem later.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "0:14-0:29", "note": "The legs change; the eyes, brain and reflexes stay normal and are flagged as important."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "1:12-1:22", "note": "Bones slide, face folds, 3 seconds, feels like a stretch."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Write it in this order: [body part or system] changes by [number]. Everything else is normal, especially [limit]. Flag the limit with a short 'keep this in mind' signal, worded freshly each time."},
   {"id": "M2", "name": "One-line teaser before each science fact",
    "description": "Each fact is announced as weird, crazy or real before it is given. This opens a 1-2 sentence curiosity gap and stops the explainer from feeling like a lecture.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "0:40", "note": "A 'something weird first' teaser before the clock illusion."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "0:44, 0:58", "note": "'Crazy part' and then 'weird part' before the cuttlefish facts."},
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "5:51", "note": "'This part is real' before the cheetah facts."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Before every science anchor, add a 3-6 word teaser that labels the fact (weird, real, the part nobody expects). Never use the same teaser twice in an episode."},
   {"id": "M3", "name": "Real-world precedent anchor",
    "description": "1-3 true facts show that a small version of the power already exists in nature, the body or technology: sprinter ground-contact research, the stopped-clock illusion, GPS relativity, fly vision, cuttlefish, face recognition. Each is credited loosely ('scientists tested', a named university, a record holder).",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "1:18-1:50", "note": "Treadmill ground-contact study."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "0:40-1:24", "note": "Three anchors in 44 s: illusion, GPS, fly."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "0:44-1:38", "note": "Cuttlefish, then the number of faces a person knows."}],
    "frequency": "3/3; 1-3 anchors in the first 100 s",
    "reuse": "Find a precedent of the form 'a [animal/organ/machine] already does a tiny version of this'. Give one checkable number. Credit a plausible source type. Verify every fact before writing it."},
   {"id": "M4", "name": "Normal-vs-you number ladder",
    "description": "A normal baseline number becomes 'now it's N', followed by 2-4 escalating comparisons the viewer can picture (highway car, race car, world-record holder, record time).",
    "evidence": [{"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "0:29-0:58", "note": "25 to 250 km/h, then car, race car, the fastest sprinter, and a 100 m time."}],
    "frequency": "1/3 explicit; the most-viewed video",
    "reuse": "For any multiplier power: baseline (an ordinary teen) -> you -> 3 comparisons in rising order -> a beat-the-record line. Put a speedometer or HUD overlay on a 3D shot while it is narrated."},
   {"id": "M5", "name": "Physics breaks it, rules repair it",
    "description": "Before the fun, the narrator shows that the naive version of the power would be lethal or useless (with time stopped, light and sound stop and air turns solid). The story then invents rules that fix each problem. This shows rigour and earns trust for the fantasy.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "1:24-2:08", "note": "Blind, deaf and stuck, then Rule 1 (a bubble around you) fixes all three."}],
    "frequency": "1/3 explicit; implicit in Shapeshift (you keep your weight)",
    "reuse": "Ask what would literally happen. Turn the 2-3 deal-breakers into rules, each with a quick test scene."}
  ],

  "limits_costs": [
   {"id": "L1", "name": "Flagged plant, flagged callback",
    "description": "A limit is planted in the first 30 s with an explicit 'this matters later' flag. It is paid off 3-4 minutes later with a callback that reuses the plant's key words ('your eyes stay normal').",
    "evidence": [{"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "0:27 -> 4:31", "note": "Plant and payoff are 4 minutes apart.", "quote": "Remember that. It matters later."}],
    "frequency": "2/3 explicit ('remember' appears 2x in 10x Faster and 5x in Shapeshift)",
    "reuse": "Use one flagged plant per episode, no more. The callback must reuse the plant's keyword so viewers feel the click."},
   {"id": "L2", "name": "Numbered rules, each demonstrated",
    "description": "There are 3-4 enumerated rules. Each one is a statement, then a physical test, then a comic consequence. Rules are discovered by trying things rather than handed over by a mentor.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "1:58-3:10", "note": "Rule 1 bubble, Rule 2 touch (basketball and rain test), Rule 3 your minutes are real (book, pizza, nap)."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "2:32-7:14", "note": "Rules 1-4: weight, study, look-not-skill, don't forget your face."}],
    "frequency": "2/3 numbered rules; 10x Faster uses one implicit rule",
    "reuse": "Use 3 rules, max 4. Each gets one 10-25 s demo scene with a gag, and at least 2 of them must be used in the climax."},
   {"id": "L3", "name": "Numbered problems: number + gag + cheap fix",
    "description": "After the 'but' turn come 3-4 enumerated problems. Each one is: name -> real number -> 2-4 vivid bodily consequences -> a low-tech workaround that looks silly but works -> a family or friend reaction. They are ordered from annoying to expensive to dangerous.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "2:41-4:24", "note": "Air (a 100x drag square law, fixed with goggles), shoes (a week per pair), food (14,000 kcal)."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "5:01-7:14", "note": "Weight, dogs (300 million vs 6 million smell sensors), details (fingerprints), identity."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Each problem gets a concrete number and a physical gag the engine can show. The fix must be ordinary (goggles, spikes, a photo in your pocket), never a new power."},
   {"id": "L4", "name": "The real problem (a turn inside the costs)",
    "description": "After the list of costs, the narrator says none of them is the real problem. The real one is a different kind: physical danger to others (stopping), time debt and loneliness (ageing alone), or losing yourself (forgetting your own face). It lands at 43-50% of a 10-min video.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "4:24 (43%)", "note": "Stopping, not speed."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "5:04 (50%)", "note": "Extra lived time adds up; fear of being stuck forever."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "6:28", "note": "Introduced as the problem nobody warned you about."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Escalate the kind of cost, not just its size: inconvenient -> expensive -> dangerous to others -> existential. The real problem should be the planted limit (L1) or the theme (L7)."},
   {"id": "L5", "name": "Chekhov density: every rule fires",
    "description": "Almost every rule, gag object and limit returns later. Counted plant-to-payoff pairs: 10x Faster 6, Stop Time 6, Shapeshift 8. The climax is solved with knowledge, not raw power.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "5:12 -> 7:07", "note": "The 300 m braking distance becomes the exact braking point in the rescue."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "2:32 -> 17:34", "note": "Keeping your weight lets you go flat as a tarp against crushing gravity."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "4:02 -> 7:37", "note": "The ice cream you saved is contrasted with the car you don't save."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Keep a plant ledger while outlining. Every plant needs a payoff, and the climax must cash at least 3."},
   {"id": "L6", "name": "Mastery through borrowed nature",
    "description": "The fix for the real problem comes from a real animal or a principle from school (cheetah claws and tail; a flat shape spreads weight). It is learned in a short montage with friends, and it gives a better technique, not a new power.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "5:42-6:31", "note": "Cheetah analogy, then spikes, leaning practice and a danger map."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "18:10", "note": "A science-class principle used in the middle of the fight."}],
    "frequency": "2/3",
    "reuse": "Find the animal or engineering principle that solves the real problem. Show it on a navy card, then give the training montage 2-3 quick tries, with one failure."},
   {"id": "L7", "name": "Theme stated as a practical rule",
    "description": "The theme is not a moral speech. It is a usable rule ('slow down before you need to', 'the outside is easy, the inside is hard'), and the climax proves it. Stop Time flips this: its rule is a temptation (nobody can see you), and the climax proves the cost of believing it.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "6:23", "note": "A braking rule doubles as the episode's theme."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "6:20", "note": "Copying the outside of a person versus the inside."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "6:10", "note": "The 'nobody can see you' logic drives the slide."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Write the theme as an instruction the hero could put on a sticky note. Plant it at 50-65%, and make the climax its proof (or its tragic violation)."}
  ],

  "escalation": [
   {"id": "E1", "name": "Scale ladder",
    "description": "The setting widens every 30-90 s: home -> school -> town -> region or public -> secret organisation or world. No setting repeats at the same scale except as a bookend.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "whole", "note": "Bedroom, school, track, town deliveries, another city, a street crisis, going viral, the van team, the highway."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "whole", "note": "Kitchen, hallway, school, zoo, park going viral, city search, garage, a 70,000-seat stadium."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "List the episode's sets in ladder order before writing. Engine sets map cleanly: bedroom/home -> classroom -> suburb/park -> city/rooftop -> stadium/void."},
   {"id": "E2", "name": "Stakes curve: flat, then a cliff",
    "description": "Stakes (rated 1-5) stay at 1 for the first 25-45% and rise to 2-3 in the costs. They jump to 5 at the crisis and stay there through the climax and cliffhanger. 10x Faster: stakes 1 until 2:41, 3 at 4:24, 5 at 6:31. Stop Time: 3 at 5:04, 5 at 7:37. Shapeshift: 3 at 6:28, 5 at 7:14.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "all", "t": "stakes_curve in data/story/beats/*.json", "note": "Each video's stakes curve is stored per beat."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "The first third should be fun, not tense. Don't fake danger early; the contrast is what makes the crisis land. Keep stakes at 5 for no more than 25% of runtime."},
   {"id": "E3", "name": "Perk montage scales up and goes public",
    "description": "Perks are ordered personal -> social -> commercial or sport -> long-range. Each is 10-35 s with a button, and the montage ends at the largest perk.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "1:50-2:41", "note": "Chores, a pizza job, soccer, lunch in another city."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "3:23-4:33", "note": "Queue, test, sleep, soccer, a kindness, a prank."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Use 4-6 perks: home chore, school, a job or money, sport or game, one kindness to plant the moral benchmark, and one big-scale flex."},
   {"id": "E4", "name": "For a while it works... then one day",
    "description": "A one-sentence time compression, then a specific day. This bridges Act 2 into the crisis at 56-63% of a 10-min video (33% in the 22-min one).",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "6:31 (63%)", "note": "A specific weekday plus a place."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "7:14 (33%)", "note": "'Keep it small' then 'until...'."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "5:40 (56%)", "note": "A specific day at school."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Use exactly one compression line, then name a day and place. Never drift into the crisis with 'and then'."},
   {"id": "E5", "name": "Moral slide ladder (anti-hero variant)",
    "description": "Instead of a rescue, the power corrupts in rungs, each justified by the same logic: payback, a small theft, a bigger theft, a heist, and finally choosing not to save someone. A best friend acts as the conscience and drifts away.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "5:40-8:35", "note": "Snack, shoes, phone, cash truck, then the crash left unfixed."}],
    "frequency": "1/3",
    "reuse": "Use it for powers that are hard to detect (invisibility, time, mind). Plant a kindness benchmark in the perk montage, and make the dark choice its mirror image."},
   {"id": "E6", "name": "Going public summons the bigger world",
    "description": "A viral clip or news story is the hinge from the personal story to the organisation. The world noticing is a consequence of the climax, not a coincidence.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "7:47", "note": "A rescue clip goes viral, then a knock at the door that night."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "7:31", "note": "2 million views, then a van 3 days later."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "8:11", "note": "News footage, then a watcher in a van."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "End the climax with a public artefact (a clip with an ironic title, a headline, CCTV) and cut to who is watching it."}
  ],

  "characters": [
   {"id": "C1", "name": "Best friend: witness, translator, conscience",
    "description": "A peer who sees the power and names it with a pop-culture reference. They react in lines of 8 words or fewer and become the emotional stake or the moral mirror later (helping with training, doubting you, or being taken).",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "3:15, 6:49, 8:28", "note": "Names the anime power, then asks if it's bad stuff, then texts about the news."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "4:29, 7:14", "note": "Milo has his own small power and is abducted (the want)."},
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "6:15", "note": "Friends build the danger-corner map."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Give the friend one tic (gamer slang, a pet theory) and one arc beat: help, doubt or be endangered. In a 10-min episode the friend gets 3-5 lines."},
   {"id": "C2", "name": "Mom: deadpan reaction and the first to notice the cost",
    "description": "Mom reacts to the logistics (shoe count, soaked clothes, cereal size, the moved mug) and is the first to notice the real cost (you look tired; that's not your chin). She closes the arc with a grounding one-liner.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "3:44, 4:19, 9:29", "note": "Shoes, cereal, then a dinner blessing."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "2:32, 4:30, 5:15", "note": "Soaked, coffee, tired."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "6:52", "note": "Notices the wrong chin."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Mom gets 2-4 one-line reactions. One of them must spot the hidden cost before the hero admits it."},
   {"id": "C3", "name": "Skeptic authority in the proof test",
    "description": "A coach, teacher or principal measures or catches you, does a double-take, and demands a rerun or gets suspicious. This is the external proof, played for comedy.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "0:58-1:18", "note": "Whistle, stopwatch, looks up, demands a rerun."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "3:40", "note": "Teacher notes a perfect score again."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "3:57", "note": "Fake principal meets the real one."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "One authority per episode, with a measurable test (stopwatch, scale, exam, camera). Show the triple look (instrument, you, instrument)."},
   {"id": "C4", "name": "The innocent: moral test object",
    "description": "A small child or ordinary bystander whose safety defines the climax: a kid chasing a ball, a kid with an ice cream, a terrified driver, a stadium crowd.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "6:31", "note": "Kid and ball."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "4:02 / 7:37", "note": "Kid's ice cream vs a crashing driver."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Plant the innocent's category early (a small kindness in the perk montage), then put a member of that category in danger at the crisis."},
   {"id": "C5", "name": "Ambiguous mentor / recurring stranger",
    "description": "A calm adult from an organisation who has been watching you. They appear in the last 25% and are morally unclear, with a visual tag (gray coat, gloves, van). They are the series spine.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "7:52", "note": "Recruits you."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "9:39", "note": "Moves in frozen time."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "10:32, 21:12", "note": "Guilty phone call, dossiers, accused."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Create our own recurring figure with a unique visual tag (do not copy the gray coat). Show more ambiguity each episode: help, then a secret, then a lie."},
   {"id": "C6", "name": "Ensemble cameo roll-call",
    "description": "Heroes from earlier episodes appear with one visual tag (hoodie colour, goggles, headphones, home-made armour, cap) and one gag line each. The audience gets callbacks; the new hero learns where they stand in the team.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "8:10-9:22", "note": "Five members, each with one gag."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "8:35-9:21", "note": "Includes the previous episode's hero."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Keep a cast bible with each past hero's tag and tic. Use at most 5 roll-call lines in 60-75 s."},
   {"id": "C7", "name": "On-the-ground antagonist",
    "description": "A peer bully (the trigger for the moral slide) or a villain pair whose powers counter the team (a touch-copier plus a time-stopper).",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "5:40", "note": "Bully triggers revenge."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "11:44", "note": "Touch-copier and time-stopper pair."}],
    "frequency": "2/3",
    "reuse": "A villain's power should counter the hero's specific rule (a copier counters touch; a time-stopper counters speed)."},
   {"id": "C8", "name": "Love interest: absent (gap)",
    "description": "None of the 3 uses romance. In the neighbouring motivational niche, adding a love counterpart was the biggest multiplier (LUST VS LOVE at 19.5x the channel median, per docs/research/script_analysis.md).",
    "evidence": [{"video": "all", "t": "-", "note": "No romantic subplot in 8,000+ narrated words."}],
    "frequency": "0/3",
    "reuse": "Optional differentiator: a crush as witness or innocent, kept light and age-appropriate (no kissing, no jealousy plots). Test it in 1 of 5 episodes."}
  ],

  "set_pieces": [
   {"id": "S1", "name": "Precision rescue (the power is the danger)",
    "description": "The power used at full strength would hurt the person you save, so the rescue needs restraint, maths and the planted rule. The kid is saved, an object is not.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "6:49-7:35", "note": "Arriving at full speed would be like a car hitting him, so you brake from exactly the planted distance."}],
    "frequency": "1/3",
    "reuse": "Ask how the power would hurt someone it touches, then build the rescue around a controlled, rule-based version. Lose a symbolic object as the small price."},
   {"id": "S2", "name": "Frozen tableau",
    "description": "A world held still (ball mid-spiral, fireworks pressed in the sky, a tyre mid-air) for awe and dread. These beats have the lowest cut rate in Shapeshift (4.7 cuts/min): long held wides and slow camera walks through still crowds.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "12:52-14:09", "note": "Frozen stadium."},
     {"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "7:12-7:37", "note": "Frozen crash on the highway."}],
    "frequency": "2/3",
    "reuse": "Cheap and spectacular in our engine: freeze actors and FX at a keyframe and dolly the camera. Use 1 per episode, 15-30 s, with 2-4 long shots."},
   {"id": "S3", "name": "Temptation heist",
    "description": "A planned crime with a clean method (frozen cameras), interrupted by an innocent in danger. The choice is the set piece.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "7:12-8:11", "note": "Cash truck on the overpass."}],
    "frequency": "1/3",
    "reuse": "Use it for anti-hero episodes. The method should be clever and rule-based, and the interruption should mirror an early kindness."},
   {"id": "S4", "name": "Infiltration in disguise",
    "description": "The hero hides inside the enemy space, one near-miss shows the danger of discovery, and the hero comes to sympathise with the people being spied on.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "8:57-11:28", "note": "A month as an equipment case."}],
    "frequency": "1/3",
    "reuse": "Works with any stealth power. Include a near-miss (a sense the power can't fool) and a moment where the hero learns the enemy is likeable."},
   {"id": "S5", "name": "Arena ensemble battle as a chain of rule payoffs",
    "description": "In a big public arena, each team member lands one signature move. The hero survives a series of attacks by applying each planted rule in turn (weight, study, flatness).",
    "evidence": [{"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "14:09-18:42", "note": "Goalpost, jersey pile, mascot, tarp."}],
    "frequency": "1/3 (the 22-min format)",
    "reuse": "For 12-min episodes or longer. List the attacks first, then assign each a rule from the episode. Never solve one with a rule that wasn't planted."},
   {"id": "S6", "name": "Try-fail comic crash",
    "description": "A low-stakes failure that teaches the limit physically (missing a turn and ending up in a pool; stuck as a laundry basket). It sits in Act 1-2 and is played for comedy.",
    "evidence": [
     {"video": "y300HjYnHPw", "t": "5:31", "note": "Hedge, two backyards, then a pool."},
     {"video": "RxAhxw6Emec", "t": "2:03", "note": "No legs, only a lid."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Use 1-2 per episode. The crash must visibly demonstrate the number just stated."},
   {"id": "S7", "name": "Power flex walk-through",
    "description": "In the last minute the hero shows total control (walks between frozen opponents, flicks the can), and then a reversal breaks it.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "YznR5NmI3bc", "t": "9:21-9:39", "note": "Hubris just before the reversal."}],
    "frequency": "1/3",
    "reuse": "Put pride before the cliffhanger: a 10-20 s flex, then the rule breaks."},
   {"id": "S8", "name": "Cut density by beat type",
    "description": "Comedy montages are the fastest-cut beats (10x Faster cold open 43.6 cuts/min, perks 27.7; Stop Time misuse 38, proof test 36.9). Explainer beats with navy cards are slower (8-15). Big set pieces are held longer (Shapeshift stadium 2.5-12 cuts/min). Spectacle comes from scale and stillness, not cutting.",
    "evidence": [{"video": "all", "t": "cuts_per_min per beat in data/story/beats", "note": "Computed from shot detection."}],
    "frequency": "3/3",
    "reuse": "Plan 25-40 cuts/min for gags and montages, 10-18 for explainers and dialogue, and 5-12 for set pieces (long moves, wides)."}
  ],

  "comedy": [

# What IF You Could Shapeshift? (RxAhxw6Emec)

IFOLOGY FILMS. Duration 22:06, 339,910 views at download. Source: YouTube auto-captions (ASR), deduplicated and merged into sentences; [music] tags removed; ASR misspellings kept unless obvious. ~4264 spoken words, ~401 in character dialogue (9%).

**Private local training data for pattern analysis only. Do not reuse lines in scripts.**

Format: `[mm:ss]` paragraph start. Narrator (2nd person) is unmarked; character lines are `> **Speaker:** line`. Speaker attribution is inferred from ASR speaker-change marks and context, so treat it as approximate. `## ` headings are the creator's YouTube chapters.


## [00:00] The discovery of a power

[00:00] There are two of your mom in the kitchen. One of them is making pancakes. The other one is standing by the fridge holding a spatula smiling way too hard. The second one is you. Your dad walks in, looks at the first mom, looks at the second mom, and very slowly puts his coffee down.

> **Dad:** Okay, I need both of you to say something only your mom would know.  

[00:21] The real mom crosses her arms. You open your mouth to answer and out comes the voice of a 7-year-old boy.

> **You (kid voice):** I'm your wife.  

[00:29] The dog starts barking. Only at you.

> **Mom:** Go to your room and give me back my face.  


## [00:35] How shapeshifting works

[00:35] So, what if you could shapeshift? What if you could become anyone or anything just by thinking about it? Here's how it works. First, the crazy part. Some animals already do a version of this. A cuttlefish can change the color and the pattern of its skin in less than a second. It can make its skin look like sand or rock or seaweed. It can even make dark stripes roll across its body like a moving cloud.

[00:58] And here's the weird part. Scientists think cuttlefish are colorblind. They match the colors around them perfectly and they can't even see those colors. Your skin does the same thing, but it doesn't stop at color. Your bones slide. Your face folds into a new face. Your hair grows or shrinks back into your head. It takes about 3 seconds and it feels like stretching after you wake up. And faces matter more than you'd think. Scientists at the University of York found that the average person knows about 5,000 faces. Your brain has a whole part that does nothing but recognize them.

[01:31] That's why a stranger with your best friend's face would fool you instantly. Which means for you, the whole world is basically a costume store. You find out you can do it when you're sick. You're playing hide-and-seek with your cousins. Your big cousin is counting to 10 and you can't find anywhere to hide. So, you crouch down next to the laundry basket in the hallway, close your eyes, and wish really, really hard that you were a laundry basket, too. Your cousin walks into the hallway. She looks behind the door, she looks under the stairs, she looks right at you twice and walks away.


## [01:40] Learning the rules

[02:03] You win hide and seek for the first time in your life, and then you try to stand up and you can't because you don't have legs. You have a lid. You stay a laundry basket for an hour. Your mom walks by and drops a pile of dirty socks on your head. When you finally pop back into a little boy covered in socks, your mom screams so loud the neighbors call to check on her.

> **Mom:** Okay. Okay. Nobody panic. Mommy's going to sit down on the floor for a minute.  

[02:29] After that, your mom makes you practice every night. Basket, boy, basket, boy. And slowly, you figure out the rule. Rule one, you keep your weight, always. If you weigh 50 kilos and you turn into a house cat, you're a 50 kilo house cat. A normal cat weighs about four. You find this out when you jump onto the couch and the couch breaks in half.


## [02:38] The limits of transformation

[02:51] Rule two, you can only become what you've really looked at. A quick look isn't enough. You have to study it. And whatever you didn't see, you get wrong. The first time you turn into your teacher, you only ever looked at her from the front. So, from the front, it's perfect. From the back, she has your messy hair and your dinosaur backpack. And rule three, you can look like anyone, but you can't become them. If you turn into a pro basketball player, you get his face, his height, and his arms. You do not get his jump shot. You still shoot like you. Oh, and your voice is the hardest part.

[03:24] It takes you years to get it right. Until then, every disguise you do talks like a little kid. Okay. A six-year-old who can turn into anything. This is going to be the best childhood ever. And for a while, it is. You never lose hide and seek again. You're the coat rack. You're the potted plant. One time you're the Christmas tree and your little cousin hangs an ornament on your nose. When you forget your permission slip, you turn into your mom in the school bathroom and sign it yourself. Her handwriting is the only thing you can't copy. The teacher says your mom writes like a 6-year-old.


## [03:30] A childhood of secrets

[03:57] You say she had a long day. When you're nine, you turn into the principal, walk into the office, and announce on the speakers that there's no homework for the rest of the week. The whole school cheers, and then the real principal walks out of the bathroom right in front of you. You stare at each other for a long time. Then you turn into a water fountain. That one doesn't really work because a water fountain doesn't usually run down the hallway. You go to the zoo and stand next to the penguins as a penguin, a 50-kilo penguin. The other penguins don't like you. The zookeeper is very confused.


## [04:30] Unexpected consequences

[04:29] And when your best friend Milo gets scared of the big kid at the bus stop, you turn into a bigger kid. Milo is the only one you ever tell because Milo has a secret, too. Milo can talk to animals, not just dogs and cats, pigeons, squirrels. One time a crow told him where a kid at school lost his house keys, and the crow was right.

> **Milo:** So you can be anything you want?  

> **You:** Anything I can see.  

> **Milo:** That's so cool. I can just talk to birds.  

> **You:** Dude, you can talk to birds.  

[05:01] You become the two weirdest kids in your whole town, and you love it. But the more you use it, the more problems you find. Problem one, being heavy is a much bigger deal than you thought. Remember rule one, you keep your weight. So the smaller you get, the more packed in you are. As a mouse, you weigh as much as a big dog. You can't fit into mouse holes because a mouse hole wasn't built for 50 kilos of mouse. You try to become a bird and fly, and you just sit there on the grass flapping. A bird is light and full of air. You are a 50-kilo pigeon.

[05:34] You are never leaving the ground.

> **Milo:** The other pigeons say you're scaring them.  

> **You:** Tell them I'm scaring me, too.  

[05:41] Problem two, dogs. You can look like anybody, but you can't smell like them. A dog's nose has up to 300 million smell sensors. Yours has about 6 million. To a dog, it doesn't matter whose face you're wearing, you smell like you. Every dog in your neighborhood knows exactly who you are, and they all think you're a liar.

[06:02] Problem three, details. Your face can copy your dad's face perfectly, but it can't copy what you never looked at, like his fingerprints. Even identical twins don't have the same fingerprints. So, when you turn into your dad to unlock his phone, it doesn't unlock. It just tells you, very politely, that you're not your dad. And the scar on his elbow, and the way he scratches his ear when he lies, and the way he says your name. You can copy the outside of a person. The inside is a lot harder. And problem four, the one nobody warned you about. The summer you turn 12, you spend 3 weeks as a lifeguard at the pool, just because you can.


## [06:31] The disappearance of Milo

[00:35] So, what if you could stop time? Here's how it works. First, something weird. Your brain already does a tiny version of this. Every time your eyes jump to something new, your brain fills in the gap and stretches that moment. And time itself isn't the same everywhere. The clocks on GPS satellites run about 38 microseconds a day faster than clocks on the ground. Einstein predicted that. It sounds like nothing, but if engineers didn't correct for it, the map on your phone would drift off by about 10 km every single day.

[01:14] Even animals feel time differently. A fly can see flickering light about four times faster than you can. That's why it's so hard to swat one. To a fly, your hand is moving in slow motion. You look exactly the same, but your brain, your eyes, your reflexes, those stay normal. Remember that. It matters later. Say your top sprint today is 25 km/h. That's a pretty normal sprint for a teenager.

[00:34] Now, it's 250. That's faster than a car on the highway. That's faster than most race cars on a street. The fastest human who ever lived, Usain Bolt, topped out at about 44 km/h. You pass him like he's standing still. 100 m? You'd run it in under a second and a half. Bolt's world record is 9.58 seconds, and nobody has beaten it since 2009.

[00:58] So, you show up to track trials just to see.

> **Coach:** Okay. On my whistle. 3 2 1.  

[01:05] He blows the whistle. He looks down at his stopwatch. He looks back up. You're already standing at the finish line, holding his water bottle.

> **Coach:** Run that again. Run that again.  

> **You:** Coach, I already ran it twice.  


## [01:18] Advantages and daily hurdles

[01:18] Now, here's why this is so hard to believe. Scientists actually tested what stops humans from running faster. They put sprinters on a special treadmill that measures every footstep. And it turns out the limit isn't how hard your legs can push. It's how fast. When an elite sprinter runs, each foot touches the ground for less than a tenth of a second. That's all the time they get to push. Your muscles just can't fire any quicker than that. Yours can. Your feet touch the ground for about a hundredth of a second. Tap. Tap. Tap.

[01:46] So fast, it sounds like a drum roll. And at first, it's the best thing that has ever happened to you. You're never late again. You speed run every chore your mom gives you. Dishes, laundry, lawn, done before the commercial break is over. You get a job delivering pizza, and you deliver across the whole town faster than the pizza place can make them.

> **Customer:** Bro, I literally just hung up the phone.  

> **You:** That'll be $14.99.  

[02:12] And the pizza shows up still steaming.

> **Customer:** Bro, you're doing the Naruto run.  

> **You:** It actually works though.  

[02:18] You join the soccer team. On your first game, you run past every single player on the field all the way to the goal. And then you look down, the ball is still back at midfield. Turns out you can only kick it as fast as your feet can find it.

> **Coach:** Maybe try defense.  

[02:33] On weekends, you run to the next city for lunch, 100 km away. It takes you less than half an hour. You're back before your food would have even been delivered. But then you start noticing the problems, and the first one is the air. At 250 km an hour, the air hitting your face is almost as fast as a category 5 hurricane.


## [02:43] The physics of extreme speed

[02:52] And here's the thing about air, it pushes back harder the faster you go. Not a little harder, way harder. Go 10 times faster and the air fights you 100 times harder. Your eyes water so hard you can't see. A bug hits your forehead like a pebble. Your hoodie tries to leave without you. Your hair has never been the same.

[03:11] So, you buy swim goggles. You tuck your arms in. You lean forward like a human bullet. It looks ridiculous. It works. And in case you're wondering, no, you're not breaking the sound barrier. The speed of sound is about 1,235 km an hour. You'd have to be about 50 times faster for that.

[03:29] So, no sonic boom, just a lot of very confused pigeons. The second problem is your shoes. Every step grinds them against the pavement at highway speed. 1 week and the soles are gone. You go through sneakers like other people go through socks.

> **Mom:** That's the fourth pair this month.  

> **You:** The ground is really rough, okay?  

[03:49] The third problem is food. Running takes about 1 calorie for every kilo you weigh for every kilometer you run. That number barely changes with speed, but you don't run one kilometer, you run everywhere. Weigh 70 kilos and run 200 kilometers in a day and that's about 14,000 calories. A normal person eats around 2,000 a day. You need a week of food every single day and that's before you count fighting all that air.

[04:14] So, you eat breakfast, then second breakfast, then a third breakfast just to be safe. Your mom starts buying cereal in boxes the size of a microwave. But here's the thing about being 10 times faster, none of that is the real problem. Going fast is easy, stopping is the problem. Remember, your eyes stay normal, so does your brain. At this speed, everything at the edge of your vision turns into a blur. Street signs, trees, people, you can only really see what's straight ahead, like looking down a tunnel. And your brain needs about a fifth of a second to react to anything.


## [04:24] Reaction time and control

[04:47] That's normal, everyone's does. But at 250 km/h, in a fifth of a second, you travel about 14 m before you even notice something is there. You find that out one morning when a dog steps onto the sidewalk. You see it, your brain goes, "Dog." And by the time your brain finishes the word, you've already jumped over it. You didn't decide to jump, you just got lucky. And once you notice something, you have to stop.

[05:12] But your shoes can only grip the ground so hard. On dry pavement, stopping from that speed takes around 300 m. That's three football fields. Turning is even worse. To turn a corner at full speed without sliding off into the street, you'd need a curve more than a kilometer wide. A normal street corner? Impossible. You find that out the hard way. You try to turn onto your street, you don't. You go straight through the neighbor's hedge, across two backyards and into an inflatable pool.

> **Friend:** Was that the any percent route?  

> **You:** Don't.  

[05:42] So, you look at the one animal that actually does this, the cheetah, the fastest land animal on Earth, up to about 100 km an hour. And this part is real. A cheetah's claws grip the ground like the cleats on a soccer shoe, and its long tail works like a rudder. When it turns, it swings that tail the other way so it doesn't fly off. Speed is only half of it. The other half is grip. You can't grow a tail, but you can get cleats. You buy the spikiest track spikes you can find. You practice leaning into turns like a motorcycle. Your friends strap a camera to your head and makes you a map of the town with every corner marked in red.


## [05:43] Mastering the slow rescue

> **Friend:** Red means slow down, like way before you see it.  

[06:23] And that's the most important rule of being fast. Start slowing down way before you need to. If you wait until you see the problem, you're already too late. For a while, it works. And then, one Saturday, you're at the top of the hill by the park, and you see it. A kid chasing a soccer ball straight into the street, and a delivery truck coming around the corner way too fast. The driver is looking at his phone.

> **Kid:** My ball!  

[06:49] You're 400 m away. Running at full speed, you'd be there in about 6 seconds, but you can't just run there. If you arrive at full speed, you can't stop. You'd fly right past him. And if you grab the kid at 250 km an hour, it's like getting hit by a car. You'd be the thing that hurts him. So, you do the math your brain was never built for. Full speed down the hill, straight line, no turns. And 300 m before the kid, you start braking. Your spikes dig in. Sparks, smoke, the pavement screams. You slow down and down

[07:23] and down, and you get there at walking speed exactly when you need to. You pick the kid up gently and step back onto the curb. The truck flies past. The soccer ball does not make it.

> **Kid:** Woah, my ball!  

> **You:** You're welcome.  

[07:39] Your spikes are melted flat. Your legs are shaking. The kids' mom is crying and hugging you, and somebody filmed the whole thing. By dinner, the video has a name: The Slowest Rescue Ever Recorded. And honestly, that's the point. That night, there's a knock at your door. You're there before the second knock, and standing on your porch is a woman in a gray coat.


## [07:54] A world of super-powered beings

> **Woman in gray coat:** The slowest rescue ever recorded. I've watched it 11 times.  

> **You:** Who are you?  

> **Woman in gray coat:** Someone who's been keeping an eye on all of you.  

> **You:** All of you?  

[08:11] Behind her, there's a black van parked on your street, and it's not empty. A kid in a blue hoodie is floating a soda can across your yard without touching it. He drops it right in your hand. Above the van, a girl in orange goggles is just hovering there, 10 m off the ground, like it's nothing.

> **Flying girl:** Nice goggles. Swim team?  

[08:30] Sitting on the hood, a guy in headphones looks at you like he already knows what you're about to say, because he does.

> **Mind-reader:** He's thinking, is that guy wearing a beetle?  

[08:39] He is. Next to the van, there's a guy in a cracked suit made of carbon fiber, bike parts, and a lot of duct tape, with a beetle horn on his helmet.

> **Beetle-suit guy:** It's a rhinoceros beetle. There's a difference.  

[08:51] And leaning on the back door, a guy in a red cap cracking his knuckles. The casts are finally off.

> **Team member:** Don't shake his hand, by the way. Trust me.  

> **Woman in gray coat:** You might have seen some of them before. One moves things with his mind. One flies. One reads minds.  

> **Woman in gray coat:** Two of them are a lot stronger than they should be. We call it Project IF.  

> **You:** And you want me?  

> **Woman in gray coat:** We have strength. We have the sky. We have the mind. What we don't have is someone who can get there first.  

[09:22] You look at the van. You look at your melted spikes. You look back at your mom standing in the doorway with a spoon of cereal halfway to her mouth.

> **Mom:** Be home for dinner.  

[09:31] And then, the woman's tablet starts flashing red. Every phone in the van goes off at the same time. The guy with the headphones takes them off. For the first time, he looks scared.

> **Mind-reader:** I can't read him. Whoever this is, I can't hear a single thought.  

> **Woman in gray coat:** That's not a drill.  

[09:46] On the screen, there's a live camera from the highway. Every car on it has stopped, not crashed, stopped, floating a few centimeters off the road, and standing in the middle of it all is one person looking straight into the camera. Six of you, one alert, and for the very first time, a villain just made [their move]. So, what would you do first if you were 10 times faster? And who do you think the villain is? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe, because this is only the beginning. Every story starts with if.

@@@@ END

# ElevenLabs: first-connect checklist

Voice (narration + character lines) uses the ElevenLabs API, called directly with `fetch` from `tools/episode.mjs` — no MCP. Run this checklist once, the first time a copy of this project has no working `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`.

Until the key is working, everything except real voice-over works: ideas, scripts, shot lists, `draft` previews, short shots with Python sound, audits, reviews and preview renders. If the user asks for a finished episode before the key works, go up to the preview (docs/pipeline/EPISODE.md step 4), then ask them for a key.

## Choices made at setup

- Narrator voice: default pick for the content language, chosen at setup — run step 3 now and confirm the pick, unless the setup answer was "audition first", in which case run step 3 as a full audition before picking anything

## Steps

1. **Get a key.** Ask the user for their ElevenLabs API key (elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys → Create API Key). Save it to `.env` at the project root as `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=...` (the `.env` file is gitignored — never commit it or print it back in full).

2. **Smoke test.** `GET https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/voices` (header `xi-api-key: <key>`) must return 200. If it 401s, the key is wrong; if it 403s with `missing_permissions`, the key is scoped — note which permissions are missing (voices/TTS access is enough to run the pipeline; `user_read` is only needed for an automatic balance check, see step 5).

3. **Pick house voices.** `tools/episode.mjs`'s `HOUSE_VOICES` needs a narrator, a male and a female voice, in the project's content language. The account's own saved voices (`/v1/voices`) may not have what's needed — search the full public library instead:
   - `GET /v1/shared-voices?language=<lang>&use_cases=narrative_story` for narrator candidates (calm/warm, not "excited" or "upbeat" — the house style is unhurried).
   - `GET /v1/shared-voices?language=<lang>&gender=male` / `&gender=female` for the secondary voices (young, casual/natural).
   - Pull 3–4 candidates per role, fetch each one's `preview_url`, and let the user pick by ear — don't choose a voice the user hasn't heard.
   - A public-library voice_id can be used directly in a TTS call without first "adding" it to the account.

4. **Measure the real cost before committing.** Credit cost per character varies by model and isn't published cleanly — measure it: call `POST /v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id}/with-timestamps` with a short (~15 s) test script in the project's content language and the chosen narrator voice and model (`eleven_v4` unless the user asks otherwise), then diff `GET /v1/usage/character-stats?start_unix=<ms>&end_unix=<ms>&include_live_requests=true` before/after (its `usage.All` series updates within a few seconds). Report the measured credits/char to the user and update the `CREDITS_PER_CHAR` constant and the Voice section of `docs/pipeline/EPISODE.md`.

5. **Balance checks.** `GET /v1/user/subscription` gives the real remaining balance, but needs the `user_read` permission. If the key doesn't have it, tell the user to check elevenlabs.io/app/subscription manually, or to create a key with that permission added, before any `/stickman` credit checkpoint.

6. **Finish.**
   - Update `HOUSE_VOICES` in `tools/episode.mjs`, the **Voice** section of `docs/pipeline/EPISODE.md`, and `public/episodes/pipetest/episode.json` (`voice.id`) if it exists.
   - Replace the memory file `project-elevenlabs-pending.md` with a short `reference` memory: "ElevenLabs connected `<date>`, narrator `<voice>`, measured `<rate>` credits/char." Update its line in `MEMORY.md`.
   - Tell the user what was checked, which voices were picked, and the measured cost.

## Costs to keep in mind

- Voice: credits/char varies by model — don't assume 1:1. See step 4 for how to measure it for real.
- Re-running `node tools/episode.mjs sections <slug>` is free; only `node tools/episode.mjs voice <slug>` spends credits, and only for sections that don't already have a `file`.
@@@@ END

# Fish Audio: thumbnail-mode first-connect checklist

Fish Audio is used only for `fish`-mode thumbnail image generation (GPT Image 2.5 via Fish's media API) — see docs/pipeline/EPISODE.md step 10. Voice does not use Fish; see `docs/ELEVENLABS_SETUP.md` for that.

Run this checklist once, the first time Fish tools are available in a session, if the thumbnail mode is `fish`. Their tool names end in `get_media_model`, `list_media_models`, `create_media_upload`, `get_credit_balance`, `list_my_workspaces`. If they appear only as deferred tools, load them with ToolSearch first.

Run this checklist again whenever the Fish account changes: the thumbnail reference keys must be reachable from the connected team.

## Choices made at setup

- Thumbnails: `fish` mode (the default) — run steps 1–2 now

## Steps

1. **Thumbnail model.**
   1. Call `get_media_model` with the `model_id` in `thumbnails/config.json` (`gpt-image-2.5-flare`).
   2. Check that it accepts the `parameters` there (16:9, 2K, medium) and `ref` image inputs, and keep its `parameter_schema`.
   3. If the model is gone or renamed, call `list_media_models`, propose the closest GPT Image model, and ask before you change `config.json`.

2. **Thumbnail references.** The `object_key`s in `thumbnails/refs/refs.json` belong to the Fish workspace the project was packed from, so upload the three images again, in order. Uploads are free.
   1. `list_my_workspaces` gives the `workspace_id`.
   2. For each `thumbnails/refs/<file>`, call `create_media_upload` with `file_name` (`ref1_paused.webp`, etc.), the exact byte size and `image/webp`.
   3. PUT the file to the returned `upload_url`: `curl.exe -X PUT -H "Content-Type: image/webp" --data-binary "@thumbnails/refs/<file>" "<upload_url>"`.
   4. Write each new `object_key` into `refs.json`, keeping the order, and set `uploaded` to today's date.

3. **Finish.**
   - Add "Last run: <date>, team <name>" under the title of this file and keep the file, for the next account change.
   - Tell the user what was checked, what changed, and what it cost.

## Costs to keep in mind

- Thumbnails (`fish` mode): 1,601 credits per 2K variant, so 3 variants are about 4.8k per episode.
- Fish AI video models are not used for episodes. A clip costs 1.4k–53k credits, and the procedural engine is free.
@@@@ END

# Plano de ação: otimizar tokens e velocidade

Escrito em 2026-11-08, depois do episódio `quem-tem-crush` (10:13, 162 planos). **Para começar numa sessão nova:** leia este arquivo inteiro e execute as fases na ordem, marcando `[x]` em cada tarefa concluída e anotando o resultado medido. Pergunte ao usuário antes de qualquer coisa que mude o PATH do Windows ou gaste créditos.

Máquina: 12 núcleos de CPU, NVIDIA RTX 3060. Ferramentas fora do PATH do terminal do Claude: `node` em `C:\Program Files\nodejs`, `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe` em `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WinGet\Packages\Gyan.FFmpeg_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe\ffmpeg-9.0.2-full_build\bin`. Até a Fase 0 resolver, prefixe os comandos com:
`export PATH="/c/Program Files/nodejs:/c/Users/G/AppData/Local/Microsoft/WinGet/Packages/Gyan.FFmpeg_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe/ffmpeg-9.0.2-full_build/bin:$PATH"`

> ## ★ Prioridades destacadas pelo usuário
>
> 1. **Cola de roteiro (tarefa 2.1).** Criar uma versão resumida de 1–2 páginas do manual de roteiro (`docs/story/STORY_BLUEPRINT.md`, 928 linhas), que hoje é lido inteiro a cada episódio. É a economia de tokens mais simples e se repete em todo episódio.
> 2. **Modelos mais fracos para ações que não precisam do mais forte (tarefa 2.4).** Rodadas de verificação, buscas e edições mecânicas não precisam do modelo principal.
> 3. **Lembrete: ensinar o usuário a escolher o modelo por ação.** O usuário pediu explicitamente para aprender a fazer isso sozinho. Ver a seção "Lembrete: ensinar a escolher modelo por ação", no fim deste documento. A sessão que executar a tarefa 2.4 **deve ensinar, não só configurar**.

**Atenção:** outra sessão do Claude pode estar produzindo outro episódio (`invasao-zumbi`) e mexendo nos mesmos arquivos do motor. Antes de editar `src/` ou `tools/`, confirme com o usuário que ela não está ativa.

## Linha de base medida (para comparar depois)

| Etapa | Antes | Depois (medido 2026-11-08) |
|---|---|---|
| `review.mjs` completo (`quem-tem-crush`, 162 planos) | 10+ min por rodada | **3 min 20 s** (stills em paralelo) |
| Rodada 2+ de revisão (quadros) | 10+ min (refazia tudo) | **27 s** com `--only` em 5 planos |
| Pré-checagem antes da revisão | não existia | **23 s** (`sheet.mjs`, 16 planos-chave) |
| Revisor, rodada 2+ | ≈ 300 mil tokens no modelo principal | só os planos alterados, em sonnet (`revisor-verificacao`); a medir no próximo episódio |
| Leitura para escrever o roteiro | blueprint + análise ≈ 65 mil tokens | cola ≈ 3 mil tokens |
| Render final | ~25 min, 1,17 GB (concorrência 4, CRF 14) | ~21% mais rápido, ~40% do tamanho (concorrência 8, CRF 18; medido em 20 s) |
| Voz (47 seções) | ~3 min em série; falha no meio = pagar de novo | 3 em paralelo (no teste falso: 22 s), salva a cada seção |
| Cada `stills.cjs` | "~30 s de bundle" | 2–3 s (cache do webpack); 11 s depois de editar `src/` |
| Retrabalho | 3 rodadas, a maioria por encenação | regras novas no `CLAUDE.md` + 3 avisos novos no audit |

---

## Fase 0 — Preparação (≈15 min)

- [x] **0.1 Git.** *Feito:* commit `baseline` (203 arquivos, 4,9 MB; `core.autocrlf false`; também ignora `public/episodes/*/raw/` e `*.pyc`). O projeto não é repositório. `git init`, criar `.gitignore` com `node_modules/`, `.venv/`, `out/`, `final/`, `.env`, `public/episodes/*/vo/`, `public/episodes/*/mix.wav`, `__pycache__/`; commit inicial "baseline". *Por quê:* desfazer com segurança e ver o que outra sessão mudou. *Verificar:* `git status` limpo.
- [x] **0.2 PATH.** *Feito:* `C:\Program Files\nodejs` adicionado ao PATH do usuário (o ffmpeg já estava). Vale depois de reiniciar o VS Code. Perguntar ao usuário se pode adicionar as duas pastas acima ao PATH do usuário (`setx` ou Configurações do Windows). *Ganho:* acaba com chamadas perdidas procurando `node`/`ffmpeg` em toda sessão. *Verificar:* num terminal novo, `node --version` e `ffmpeg -version`.

## Fase 1 — Velocidade (código pequeno, ganho grande)

- [x] **1.1 Stills em paralelo.** *Feito:* pool de páginas (`--parallel N`, padrão 4) e a composição é resolvida uma vez por props. 40 stills: 32 s em série → 13,7 s com 4 (2,3×). Com 6 fica mais lento (31 s; a GPU satura). Quadros idênticos (PSNR 92 dB). `tools/stills.cjs` renderiza um quadro por vez no laço `for (const j of jobs)`. Trocar por um pool de N páginas (padrão 4, opção `--parallel N`) usando o mesmo `browser`. *Ganho esperado:* `review.mjs` de ~12 min para ~3–4 min. *Verificar:* cronometrar `node tools/review.mjs quem-tem-crush` antes e depois; os arquivos em `out/quem-tem-crush/review/` saem iguais.
- [x] **1.2 Revisão incremental.** *Feito:* `review.mjs <slug> --only id,id` (ids ou índices). Manifest guarda `timingHash`/`shotIds` e recusa `--only` se a voz ou a lista de planos mudou. `manifest.only` diz ao revisor o que mudou; `REVIEWER_BRIEF.md` ganhou a seção "Verification rounds". Pipetest: completo 35 s → `--only` 2 planos 15 s (quase tudo é o bundle de ~10 s, que a 1.5 ataca). Obs.: o manifest antigo do `quem-tem-crush` não tem hash; a 1ª rodada lá precisa ser completa. `tools/review.mjs` aceita só `<slug>` e refaz tudo. Adicionar `--only c8,r6,...` (ids de plano): renderiza e lista no `manifest.json` só esses planos (mais os eventos que os envolvem); o resto do manifest fica como estava. *Ganho:* rodadas 2+ em ~1 min. *Verificar:* `--only c8` gera só `shot_007*.jpg`.
- [x] **1.3 Render final mais rápido e leve.** *Feito:* padrão concorrência = núcleos − 4 (8 aqui) e CRF 18, com `--concurrency`/`--crf`. Trecho de 20 s: concorrência 4 → 85 s, 6 → 74 s, 8 → 67 s, 10 → 66 s. CRF 18 = 39% do tamanho do CRF 14, SSIM 0,994, sem diferença visível. Aceleração de hardware não testada. `tools/build-episode.mjs` linha 45 fixa `--concurrency=4 --crf=14`. Trocar para concorrência padrão `Math.max(2, os.cpus().length - 4)` (8 nesta máquina) e CRF 18, com `--crf N` e `--concurrency N` para sobrescrever. *Ganho:* render ~40% mais rápido, arquivo ~metade (≈600 MB). *Verificar:* renderizar `quem-tem-crush --from 0 --to 60` com o antigo e o novo; comparar tempo, tamanho e um quadro lado a lado.
  - Opcional: testar se o Remotion 4 instalado aceita aceleração de hardware no Windows/NVIDIA. Se não aceitar, não forçar.
- [x] **1.4 Voz em paralelo.** *Feito sem gastar créditos:* 3 chamadas ao mesmo tempo (`voice.parallel`), com nova tentativa em 429/5xx (respeita `retry-after`). Também corrigi um bug: antes, o `sections.json` só era salvo no fim, então uma falha no meio fazia pagar de novo as seções já prontas; agora salva a cada seção. Testado com um ElevenLabs falso (`--import` de um mock que troca o `fetch`) sobre as 47 seções do `quem-tem-crush`: máx. 3 simultâneas, 14 erros 429 recuperados, 1 recusa isolada (46/47 salvas), a nova execução chamou só a que falhou, `align` sem diferença de palavras. **Confirmado com a API real em 2026-11-09 (`menu-corpo`): 49/49 seções em 104 s, 3 em paralelo, `align` sem diferença de palavras.** `tools/episode.mjs`, laço `for (const id of ids)` (~linha 302) chama `synthesize` uma seção por vez. Trocar por um pool de 3 chamadas simultâneas (opção `voice.parallel` no `episode.json`), com nova tentativa automática em erro 429 (limite da API). Manter a ordem do `sections.json`. *Ganho:* voz em <1 min. *Verificar:* rodar num episódio de teste curto (pipetest) e conferir que `align` não acusa diferença de palavras. **Gasta créditos: pedir OK ao usuário.**
- [x] **1.5 Reaproveitar o bundle.** *Medido e descartado:* o cache do webpack já deixa o bundle em 1,8–2,9 s quando nada mudou (11 s depois de editar `src/`). Os "30 s" eram do cache frio. Guardar o bundle economizaria ~2 s por chamada e exigiria sincronizar os 333 MB de `public/`, então não compensa. `stills.cjs` chama `bundle()` a cada execução (~30 s). Guardar o bundle em `out/.bundle` e reaproveitar quando nenhum arquivo em `src/` ou `public/episodes/<slug>/` mudou (comparar a data de modificação mais recente). *Ganho:* ~30 s em cada chamada de stills/review. *Verificar:* a 2ª chamada seguida começa a renderizar sem a linha "bundled in".

## Fase 2 — Menos tokens

- [x] **★ 2.1 Cola de roteiro (prioridade do usuário).** *Feito em 2026-11-08:* `docs/story/COLA_ROTEIRO.md` (100 linhas, ~10 KB, ≈3 mil tokens) substitui a leitura do blueprint (76 KB, ≈50 mil tokens) **e** do `script_analysis.md` (52 KB, ≈15 mil) no passo 2. `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/commands/stickman.md` e `tools/pack/fresh/stickman.md` apontam para a cola. Economia: ≈60 mil tokens por episódio. Criar `docs/story/COLA_ROTEIRO.md` (1–2 páginas) a partir do `STORY_BLUEPRINT.md` (928 linhas): tabela de batidas do 10:00 com tempos, fórmula de premissa, checklist §9 em forma curta, regras de tags §6.9 e números §6.4. No `CLAUDE.md` (passo 2 do episódio longo): "leia a cola; abra o blueprint completo só na seção que precisar". *Ganho:* dezenas de milhares de tokens por episódio.
- [x] **2.2 Kit do gerador de episódio.** *Feito:* `tools/episodes/kit.py` reúne `A`, `S`, `C`, `cam`, `walk`, `crush`, `SW`, `episode()` (narrador e vozes da casa por padrão; música como pares (id, clima)), `load_timing()` (start/word/at/fmt), `resolve_countdowns()` genérico (veio do zumbi), `clean` e `write`. `quem_tem_crush.py` usa o kit; regenerado, o `episode.json` saiu idêntico (diff vazio). Criado `_modelo.py` com as 17 batidas. `invasao_zumbi.py` não foi mexido, porque pode estar em produção no outro PC. Passo 3 do `CLAUDE.md` e `/stickman` atualizados. Os helpers estão dentro de `tools/episodes/quem_tem_crush.py` (627 linhas): `A`, `S`, `C`, `cam`, `crush`, `shot_block`, e o cálculo do cronômetro a partir de `timing.json`. Mover para `tools/episodes/kit.py`, fazer `quem_tem_crush.py` importar dele, e criar `tools/episodes/_modelo.py` (esqueleto com as 17 batidas comentadas). *Verificar:* regenerar `quem-tem-crush` e confirmar que o `episode.json` sai idêntico (`git diff` vazio).
- [x] **2.3 Pré-checagem barata.** *Feito:* `tools/sheet.mjs <slug> [ids]`; sem ids escolhe sozinho (abertura, 1º plano de cada set, 2 últimos; máx. 16). `quem-tem-crush`: 16 planos em 23 s, uma imagem só. Passo 7.2 do `CLAUDE.md` atualizado. Criar `tools/sheet.mjs <slug> <id,id,...>`: renderiza um still por plano (em ~70% da duração) e monta um mosaico 4×N em `out/lab/<slug>_sheet.jpg`. No `CLAUDE.md`, passo 7, antes do `review.mjs`: "rode a sheet em ~16 planos-chave (abertura, cada set novo, clímax, gancho) e corrija o óbvio". *Ganho:* pega a maior parte dos erros antes da revisão de 162 planos.
- [x] **★ 2.4 Modelo certo para cada ação (prioridade do usuário).** *Feito em 2026-11-08:* lição dada (comandos conferidos na documentação oficial). O usuário criou `.claude/agents/revisor-verificacao.md` (`model: sonnet`, `effort: medium`) e acertou o teste: clímax → opus; conferir correções → sonnet/medium; render → sem ajudante. O `CLAUDE.md`, passo 7.4, usa esse ajudante na rodada 2+; ele também vai no pacote portátil. No `CLAUDE.md`, passo 7: rodada 1 da revisão completa com o modelo padrão; rodadas 2+ com `review.mjs --only <planos alterados>`, briefing focado nos itens abertos, e o revisor num modelo menor. Estender a mesma lógica às outras ações (tabela abaixo). O usuário pediu essa economia em 2026-11-08 **e quer aprender a fazer isso sozinho** — ver o lembrete no fim. *Ganho:* rodadas 2+ de ~300 mil para ~50–100 mil tokens, e menos custo em buscas e tarefas mecânicas.

  | Ação no pipeline | Precisa do modelo forte? | Sugestão |
  |---|---|---|
  | Escrever o roteiro, decidir encenação e clímax | Sim | modelo principal da sessão |
  | Revisão independente, rodada 1 (achar problemas) | Sim | modelo principal |
  | Rodadas 2+ da revisão (conferir se foi corrigido) | Não | modelo intermediário |
  | Buscar arquivo, procurar texto no código | Não | agente de busca rápido / modelo pequeno |
  | Tradução de docs, edições mecânicas em lote | Não | modelo intermediário |
  | Gerar quadros, rodar audit, build | Não usa modelo | só ferramentas; não delegar a agente |

## Fase 3 — Evitar retrabalho

- [x] **3.1 Regras novas no `CLAUDE.md`** *Feito:* bloco "Staging traps from quem-tem-crush" em Hard-won rules (a de números saiu, porque a 3.2 resolveu). (seção "Hard-won rules"), cada uma com uma linha de causa e solução:
  - **Pose parcial volta o resto para "em pé":** passe a pose completa num personagem sentado.
  - **`sitFloor` afunda os pés ~0,4 m:** para sentar no chão ou no meio-fio, use `sit` em cima de um `crate` (h 0,45) ou `kneel`.
  - **Prop `smoke` perto da câmera parece pedra:** use puffs pequenos (`size` ~0,25, `n` 60, `wind`) e longe da linha de visão.
  - **Brilho aditivo some de dia, em qualquer cor:** use `glow` sólido ou o selo `crush`.
  - **Flow precisa dos mesmos props e atores nos dois planos;** se não, eles somem no meio do movimento.
  - **`insert` de mão dá erro no audit:** use `close` com `focus: 'handR'` e `dist` curto.
  - **Dois atores muito distantes no mesmo enquadramento automático deixam o quadro vazio:** separe os planos ou use câmera explícita.
  - **Diálogo:** confira que quem fala está de frente; `over: '<ouvinte>'` resolve a maioria.
  - **Números em cards formatam em inglês** até a tarefa 3.2.
- [x] **3.2 Números em PT-BR.** *Feito:* conferido no still: `stat` 0,1 → "0,1"; `compare` 5000 → "5.000", selo "1.000×". Episódios antigos re-renderizados também mudam. `src/cards/kit.tsx:86` e `src/episode/overlays.tsx:16` usam `toLocaleString('en-US')`. Trocar para `'pt-BR'` (todo o conteúdo do canal é PT-BR desde 2026-11-08). *Verificar:* `npx remotion still CardLab` de um `stat` com 0,1 e de um `compare` com 5000 mostra "0,1" e "5.000". Avisar o usuário: muda também os episódios antigos se forem re-renderizados.
- [x] **3.3 Tamanho de objeto na mão.** *Feito:* `hold: { R: 'flower', scaleR: 2 }` (também `scaleL`), escala pela palma. Conferido num still lado a lado (normal × 2). `HandProp` (`src/sets/props.tsx:12`, usado em `src/engine/Stickman.tsx:457`) só recebe `type`. Aceitar `hold: { R: 'flower', scaleR: 2 }` ou `holdScale`, para objetos que a narração destaca. *Verificar:* still do Caio com a flor em `scale` 2.
- [x] **3.4 Avisos novos no audit** (opcional, `src/episode/audit.ts`). *Feito:* `pose` (pose parcial depois de sentar ou ajoelhar) e dois de `continuity` no flow (elenco diferente; props diferentes). Testados num episódio sintético: os três disparam. No `quem-tem-crush` não acusam nada novo (7 avisos antes e depois).
  - **Pose parcial num ator sentado:** avisar quando ela faria o ator levantar.
  - **Props diferentes num flow:** avisar quando os props mudam entre dois planos unidos por flow.

## Fase 4 — Fechar

- [x] **4.1 Medir de novo** *Feito:* tabela de linha de base acima atualizada. no `quem-tem-crush` (sem regravar voz): tempo do `review.mjs`, do `review.mjs --only` com 5 planos, do render de 60 s. Anotar na tabela de linha de base acima ("antes → depois").
- [x] **4.2 Testes:** *Feito:* typecheck ok, 21/21, audit com 0 erros (7 avisos, os mesmos de antes). `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (21/21), `node tools/qa.cjs audit quem-tem-crush` com 0 erros.
- [x] **4.3 Cópia portátil:** *Feito:* 197 arquivos, 3,7 MB; inclui cola, kit e `revisor-verificacao`. `node tools/pack/pack.mjs` (o `CLAUDE.md` pede para reempacotar depois de mudar motor, ferramentas ou docs).
- [x] **4.4 Commit** *Feito:* um commit por tarefa (`git log`). por fase (`git commit`), mensagem curta dizendo o ganho medido.

## ★ Lembrete: ensinar a escolher modelo por ação

**Para a sessão que executar a tarefa 2.4:** o usuário pediu para *aprender* a escolher o modelo por ação, não só que fique configurado. Pare antes de configurar, explique em português simples, com exemplos deste projeto, e deixe o usuário fazer pelo menos uma das configurações. Confirme cada nome de comando e de opção na documentação do Claude Code antes de ensinar (o agente `claude-code-guide` responde isso); não ensine nada de memória.

O que ensinar, em ordem:
1. **Trocar o modelo da sessão inteira:** o comando `/model`, que o usuário já usou em 2026-11-08 (`/model opus`). Quando vale a pena: roteiro e clímax no modelo forte; sessão de ajustes mecânicos num menor.
2. **Escolher o modelo de um subagente na hora de criar:** o parâmetro de modelo da ferramenta de agentes. É o que o Claude usa ao disparar o revisor. Mostrar como pedir ("rode o revisor da rodada 2 num modelo menor").
3. **Fixar o modelo de um tipo de agente:** criar um arquivo em `.claude/agents/` (ex.: `revisor-verificacao.md`) com o modelo definido no cabeçalho. Assim, toda rodada de verificação já usa o modelo certo sem precisar lembrar. Fazer junto com o usuário.
4. **Modelo padrão dos subagentes:** a configuração que define o modelo usado por padrão quando nenhum é pedido. Confirmar o nome exato na documentação.
5. **Esforço (effort):** além do modelo, dá para pedir menos ou mais esforço de raciocínio numa tarefa; explicar quando usar cada um.
6. **Regra prática para o usuário:** criar e decidir → modelo forte; conferir, buscar e repetir → modelo menor; tarefas que só rodam ferramentas → não precisam de agente nenhum.

No fim, pedir ao usuário que diga com as próprias palavras qual modelo usaria em 2–3 ações do pipeline, para confirmar que ficou claro.

## Já resolvido nesta produção (não refazer)

- Deixas `@palavra` com acento falhavam em silêncio: corrigido em `src/episode/cue.ts`, `src/episode/audit.ts` e `tools/sfx/episode_audio.py`.
- O `cast` do episódio apagava a roupa do personagem (merge raso): corrigido em `src/episode/resolve.ts`.
- Overlay `crush` (selo rosa com %): `src/overlays/CrushMeter.tsx`, já com proteção contra sair do quadro.
- `episode.mjs check`: bloqueia a voz se houver colchete aberto, SSML ou dígito na narração.

**Medição 2026-11-09 (`menu-corpo`, 194 planos):** revisão rodada 1 (`general-purpose`, modelo da sessão) ≈ 296 k tokens / 87 chamadas / 7 min; rodada 2 (`revisor-verificacao`, sonnet, `review.mjs --only` com 52 planos) ≈ 88 k tokens / 63 chamadas / 1,3 min.

# Setting up a new machine (git clone)

The repo carries the whole system: engine, tools, docs, generators, episode specs, the user's memory (`docs/memory/`) and the **paid** ElevenLabs audio (`public/episodes/*/vo/*.mp3` + `*.align.json`). It does not carry videos (`final/`, `out/`), installed packages, or the API key.

## 1. Install (once)
- **Windows** (the tools call `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`).
- **Node.js 22+**, **Git**, **Python 3.11+**.
- **FFmpeg** with `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on the PATH (e.g. `winget install Gyan.FFmpeg`).
- **Claude Code**.
- Optional: **yt-dlp** on the PATH, only to refresh competitor title lists (`tools/ideas/novelty.py refresh`).

## 2. Get the project
```
git clone <repo url> D:\stickman-2
cd D:\stickman-2
npm ci
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
npx remotion browser ensure
npm test
```
`npm test` must end with every self-test passing.

## 3. The ElevenLabs key
Create `.env` in the project root (it is gitignored, never commit it):
```
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=<your key>
```

## 4. Use it
Open the folder in Claude Code. In the first session, Claude copies `docs/memory/` into its memory folder (CLAUDE.md, first lines). Then:
```
/stickman E Se Você <tema>
```
It runs the whole pipeline with the house rules: acid tone, fast pacing, 4+ clips of ~90 s for shorts. It stops once before spending voice credits. The video, `.srt` and `- cortes.txt` land in `final/`.

## Notes
- **Old episodes rebuild without new credits.** `node tools/build-episode.mjs <slug>` sees the missing `.wav` and rebuilds them from the saved mp3s (`episode.mjs pace`); no ElevenLabs call.
- `final/README.md` (the episode list) is not in git; a build or `/stickman` recreates it.
- Thumbnails in `chatgpt` mode need nothing extra. `fish` mode needs the Fish Audio MCP (`docs/FISH_SETUP.md`).
@@@@ END

# House Style: 3D Stickman "What If" Films

This style is built from IFOLOGY FILMS, Ifverse Tales, Last Soul Origin, Monk Mode Films and Day One Films. Our main character is modelled on IFOLOGY's lead, with our own gray wardrobe.
- The full script and packaging research is in `research/script_analysis.md`.
- HD reference contact sheets are in `research/reference_frames/`. They come from the user's three top picks:
  - "What IF You Were 10x Faster?"
  - "What IF You Could Stop Time?"
  - "What IF You Could Shapeshift?"

## 1. What the reference channels do

| | IFOLOGY / Ifverse ("What If", longform) | Day One / Monk Mode (motivational) | Last Soul Origin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medium | 3D, low-poly toon | 2D vector on black | 3D silhouette, soft light |
| Length | 7–24 min | 2.5–4 min | 3–5.5 min |
| Avg shot | 2.9–5.5 s (IFOLOGY "Stop Time": 2.9 s) | 11–26 s | ~5 s |
| Voice | 2nd person present, 180–190 wpm (IFOLOGY), ~110 wpm (Ifverse) | almost none: text cards plus an inner voice | dialogue captions |
| Top video | 4.5M (Ifverse, "Reaction Time 10x"), 813K (IFOLOGY, "10x Faster") | 5.1M ("DISCIPLINE") | 747K ("1 MINUTE") |

**Our lane:** the IFOLOGY/Ifverse "What If" format, 8–10 min, numbers in the title. This has the steadiest views and carries mid-roll ads. See the research doc §7 for the beat sheet and topics.

## 2. Character: the hero

The IFOLOGY lead's construction, in our own wardrobe: a gray quarter-zip jacket since 2026-11-08 (it was red, before that purple).
- **Head:** a big matte-black sphere (r 0.212 m) with a **crisp cream crescent** (`#f6e7c6`) on its upper-left silhouette edge, plus a thin black contour. No neck: the head sits on the hood.
- **Face:** tiny thin white line art in the lower-centre of the head.
  - Eyes are small vertical ovals, or ∩ arcs when happy or closed.
  - Brows appear only when emotional; the mouth is a thin curve.
  - When shocked, the eyes turn into white discs with pupils.
  - Never draw big cartoon features. The black head should dominate.
- **Body:** fitted quarter-zip jacket in gray `#8b8f98` with gold zip-pull trim `#c9a227`, no hood, a short chest zip, and a small stand-up collar. Charcoal pants `#2b2f3a`, off-white sneakers `#f4f1ea`. No other character wears gray.
- **Limbs:** thin black sticks with black mitten hands (with thumb). Two-band cel shading on the cloth, cream edge highlight, thin black inverted-hull outline.
- **Proportions:** about 1.8 m tall. Head diameter ≈ 1.25× jacket width. Legs are long and thin.
- **When powered:** the crescent turns lavender (`#d2b2ff`), the face lines glow purple, and you get a purple aura, sparks and crackles.

All of this is code in `src/engine/Stickman.tsx` and `src/cast.ts`. Change the wardrobe in `cast.ts`.

## 3. World

- **Low-poly suburb:** pastel two-storey houses with gable roofs, white trim and light-blue glass; green lawns; bumpy rounded hedges; round-blob trees; beige sidewalks with joints; blue-grey asphalt with a yellow dashed centre line and white edge lines.
- **Light:** bright late afternoon. The sky runs from blue to a pale horizon. Shadows are soft but clear, from one sun.
- **Shading:**
  - Environments use 3-band toon shading.
  - Characters use 2 bands plus the rim crescent.
  - No tone mapping, so the colours you type are the colours you get.
- **Grade:** a heavy IFOLOGY vignette and fine film grain (`src/overlays/Grade.tsx`).

## 4. Camera and editing

- **Lens:** fov 28–35 (no wide-angle distortion), mostly at eye or chest height. Use a low angle for hero and power moments, and an ECU for reactions.
- **Shot length:** cut every 2.5–5 s; action beats 0.5–1.5 s.
- **Motion:** every shot moves a little (push-in, drift, small shake). Use impulse shake on impacts.
- **Speed shots:** use a two-layer render.
  - The world goes on its own canvas with a strong horizontal blur.
  - The hero renders sharp on a transparent canvas, with real shadows from a `shadowMaterial` ground.
  - Anime speed lines sit between the two layers, with afterimages behind him.
- **Flashes:** short (0.1–0.2 s) white or purple flashes on surges and impacts only.

## 5. On-screen graphics

- **Stat callout** (IFOLOGY gold): a chunky serif number (Bree Serif) with a gold gradient and a dark purple drop-shadow, a gold underline, and a cream condensed label (Barlow Condensed 800). Numbers count up. See `src/overlays/Stat.tsx`.
- **Energy:** 2D lightning arcs that leave the silhouette outward (never across the face), plus 3D sparks and glow (`src/overlays/Energy.tsx`, `src/engine/fx.tsx`).
- **Later** (not built yet): IFOLOGY's navy "blueprint" explainer cards with white line-art and gold numbers, title cards, chapter labels.

## 6. Sound

Every sound is generated in Python (`tools/sfx/sfxlib.py`). No samples are used.
- **Layers:** ambience (air, distant traffic, birds), foley (cloth, clicks, gulp), power (reverse swell, heartbeat, sub drop, riser, crackle), impacts (boom, debris, leaves, distant sonic boom), speed (wind roar, footfalls, pass-by whooshes), and UI (ticks, chime).
- **Biggest hit:** the main action (the launch), not the setup.
- **Master:** about −14 dB RMS, peak −1 dBFS.
